question: Does an average input-output sensitivity measure identify which pretrained Vision Transformer components should be fine-tuned, and do attention and feed-forward components outperform normalization components because their measured plasticity is higher?

key_findings.claim: The paper defines component plasticity as an average finite-difference expansion ratio across distinct embedded source/downstream image pairs; its label "non-smooth" means only that this average ratio exceeds one, not that the component is non-differentiable or lacks a finite local Lipschitz constant.
key_findings.evidence: Definition 1 sets P(f)=E[||f(x)-f(y)||_F/||x-y||_F], distinguishes P(f)<1 from P(f)>1, and explicitly calls the latter low-smoothness or non-smooth "by abuse of language." Because P(f) is an average lower bound on a worst-case Lipschitz constant, P(f)>1 establishes average expansion on the sampled pair distribution, not mathematical nonsmoothness.

anchors.section: 3, Plasticity measure and Connection to finetuning

key_findings.claim: The theoretical section derives separate upper bounds for LayerNorm, feed-forward linear maps, and bounded-domain multi-head attention, then predicts the order MHA > FC1 approximately FC2 > LN2 approximately LN1 from the relative looseness of those bounds.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 bounds LayerNorm by ||gamma||_infinity/sigma; Proposition 2 bounds a feed-forward linear layer by ||W||_2; Propositions 3 and 4 bound attention using head projection norms, token radius or image energy, and sequence length. The paper then assumes comparable parameter-entry ranges and practical spectral norms above one to order the bounds.

key_findings.claim: The bound comparison is not a proof that actual component plasticities have the claimed order, and the paper's own numerical audit shows the attention bound is orders of magnitude above the observed quantity.
key_findings.evidence: An upper bound can be larger while its underlying quantity is smaller, and the entry-range comparability premise is informal. Appendix E.1.1 evaluates the bounds at n=197, H=12, and radius 19.4; it reports the attention bound remains around order 10^6 and says the empirical component plasticities are on much closer scales, attributing the gap to the difficulty of bounding self-attention.

key_findings.claim: Across the reported supervised ViTs and eleven downstream image datasets, the measured average-sensitivity order is consistently MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1, with MHA and feed-forward ratios above one and LayerNorm ratios below one.
key_findings.evidence: The study pairs embeddings from 12,800 ImageNet-1k images with embeddings from CIFAR-10/100, five severity-5 CIFAR-10-C corruptions, DomainNet Clipart/Sketch, Flowers102, and Pets. Figures 3 and 8-17 report the same order across ViT-Base and ViT-Huge layers; ViT-Huge has sequence length 257 versus 197 for Base and larger measured MHA plasticity.

anchors.section: E.1.2, Plasticity Experiments of All Benchmarks

key_findings.claim: The DINOv3-7B and GPT-2 extensions reproduce the descriptive plasticity order but do not test the central claim that this order predicts better component-wise fine-tuning outside supervised image classification.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 measures DINOv3 using ImageNet-22k/CIFAR-10 and GPT-2 using AG News/WikiText-103 and reports MHA followed by FC1, FC2, and norms. No DINOv3 or GPT-2 component-fine-tuning outcomes accompany this extension; Appendix E.1.3 also characterizes AG News as a proxy for unavailable GPT-2 pretraining data.

anchors.section: 5.1, Beyond supervised vision transformers and Figure 4
E.1.3, Extension to DINOv3 and GPT-2

key_findings.claim: On the eleven-dataset SGD aggregate, MHA and FC1 are nearly tied and all three high-plasticity groups outperform either LayerNorm group, but full fine-tuning remains the strongest average baseline.
key_findings.evidence: Table 8 averages are MHA 90.75, FC1 90.68, FC2 90.31, LN2 89.93, and LN1 89.82 top-1 accuracy, versus 90.90 for full fine-tuning and 64.22 for linear probing. Table 1's Wilcoxon signed-rank annotations state MHA differs at 5% from each group except FC1.

key_findings.claim: The headline rank is an aggregate tendency, not a dataset-universal component ordering.
key_findings.evidence: In Table 8, FC1 exceeds MHA on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Gaussian Noise, Snow, and Flowers102; FC2 is best among components on Sketch; LN2 is best among components on Gaussian Noise and Flowers102; and LN1 is best on Pets. Full fine-tuning is higher than every component on Contrast, Clipart, Sketch, and Pets and has the highest overall mean, while component tuning wins the other seven cells.

key_findings.claim: The comparison between high-plasticity linear/attention components and low-plasticity LayerNorm components is severely confounded by trainable capacity and optimizer-state memory.
key_findings.evidence: Table 5 lists 28M trainable transformer parameters (33% of ViT-Base) for each of MHA, FC1, and FC2 but only 18K (0.02%) for either LayerNorm group. Table 6 reports 220 MB of gradients plus SGD state for each 28M group versus 0.14 MB for LayerNorm. Thus the paper's cross-family accuracy result does not isolate plasticity at matched parameter or memory budget; only MHA/FC1/FC2 and LN1/LN2 are internally budget-matched.

key_findings.claim: The observed gradient-norm and loss dynamics are compatible with the proposed optimization story but do not establish that input plasticity causes those dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 orders component gradient norms like the plasticity metric and shows steeper validation-loss descent for high-plasticity groups on Sketch, while Figures 21-53 repeat curves across datasets. The showcased central trajectories are selected from the run attaining the highest accuracy, and no intervention changes P(f) while holding module identity, trainable count, parameterization, and optimizer fixed.

anchors.section: 5.2, Interplay between plasticity and optimization, Figure 5

key_findings.claim: The qualitative ordering persists under Adam and under a 1,000-example protocol, although component winners and uncertainty remain heterogeneous.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2's four-dataset Adam averages are MHA 82.2, FC1 81.4, FC2 81.7, LN2 79.4, and LN1 79.2. Table 3's 1,000-example averages are 94.4, 93.8, 93.3, 93.4, and 93.0 respectively; the per-dataset rows include individual LayerNorm or FC winners and standard deviations that can overlap.

anchors.section: 5.2, Extension to Adam and low-data regimes

key_findings.claim: The only larger-model component-fine-tuning table is a single DomainNet Clipart experiment, so scale generality is much narrower than the plasticity analysis.
key_findings.evidence: Table 9 reports ViT-Base MHA/FC1/FC2/LN2/LN1 of 76.9/75.7/75.9/73.6/74.0 and ViT-Large of 78.4/77.3/78.3/76.1/76.8 on Clipart. No eleven-dataset ViT-Large/Huge component-fine-tuning matrix is reported; ViT-Huge is used for sensitivity measurement only.

key_findings.claim: FC2 plasticity is not measured on the activations that FC2 normally receives, weakening the functional comparability of the five component scores.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix D.3 says all components receive embedded sequences in R^d except FC2, whose native input is in R^(4d); instead of passing the actual output of FC1/GeLU, the implementation lifts each embedded token to R^(4d) by padding the remaining coordinates with zeros. This evaluates FC2 on a synthetic subspace and can change its finite-difference ratio.

key_findings.claim: The experiments are broad in run count but narrow in task family and compute footprint.
key_findings.evidence: The central fine-tuning sweep uses four learning rates, three seeds, five component groups, and eleven image-classification datasets, totaling about 1,000 runs. Appendix C estimates 3,700 GPU-hours, up to $40,000 cloud cost, and about 259 kgCO2eq under a France-region electricity assumption; segmentation, detection, generation, adversarial evaluation, and actual LLM component tuning are absent.

method.core_idea: Rank native Transformer component groups by an empirical average input-output expansion ratio, connect that ratio to Lipschitz-style bounds and parameter-gradient intuition, then test whether fine-tuning each group in isolation follows the same rank.
method.mechanism: Images from a pretraining distribution and a downstream distribution are embedded by a frozen pretrained transformer. For each MHA, FC1, FC2, LN1, and LN2 module across depth, the study averages ||f(x)-f(y)||_F/||x-y||_F over distinct sequence pairs. Separate analytic upper bounds motivate a predicted order. It then freezes the backbone except one repeated component type across all blocks, randomly initializes the classifier, sweeps four learning rates and three seeds, selects checkpoints by validation accuracy, and compares test accuracy, learning-rate/seed robustness, gradient norms, and loss curves.
assumptions: Average expansion between source and downstream embeddings is a meaningful proxy for a component's ability to adapt its weights during supervised fine-tuning.
The cited relationship between input Jacobians and parameter gradients transfers to these heterogeneous modules strongly enough to motivate component selection.
Component-wise upper bounds can be compared despite different tightness, dimensions, head structure, and informal comparability of parameter-entry ranges.
LayerNorm token means and standard deviations can be treated as position-specific constants with a positive common lower bound for Proposition 1.
Attention inputs lie in a bounded token ball, or originate from images of uniformly bounded total energy through a bounded embedding operator.
Practical attention spectral norms exceed one and the sequence-length factors dominate enough to make its bound the loosest.
Source/downstream finite differences capture task-relevant shift rather than arbitrary scale or representation geometry.
Zero-padded embedded tokens are a representative domain on which to evaluate FC2 even though FC2 normally consumes nonlinear FC1 activations.
Comparing 28M-parameter attention/FC groups with 18K-parameter LayerNorm groups can reveal a plasticity effect despite the capacity and memory gap.
The four-rate sweep, common optimizer family, and three seeds are sufficient to compare differently scaled parameter groups fairly.
Eleven supervised image-classification transfers represent broader Transformer adaptation behavior.
A descriptive DINOv3/GPT-2 sensitivity replication is evidence of architectural generality even without corresponding fine-tuning interventions.

techniques.role: Measures a component's mean output expansion across embedded source/downstream sequence pairs.
Derives module-specific upper bounds for LayerNorm, dense maps, and attention to motivate a rank.
Makes standard dot-product attention analyzable on a compact input domain.
Replaces the radius-heavy attention bound with a bound using image energy and embedding spectral norm.
Fine-tunes exactly one native component type in every Transformer block while freezing other backbone parameters.
Tests each dataset/component pair over four rates and three random seeds.
Reports test accuracy from the checkpoint with highest validation accuracy for each run.
Compares plasticity order with parameter-gradient magnitude and validation-loss descent.
Repeats selected component comparisons with AdamW after rescaling the rate grid.
Restricts training to 1,000 examples and 2,500 steps to probe data scarcity.
Computes the descriptive metric on DINOv3-7B and GPT-2-124M.
Tests aggregate paired differences between MHA and other groups over eleven benchmark values.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet-22k-pretrained ViT-Base/Huge, source embeddings from 12,800 ImageNet-1k images, downstream embeddings from eleven image-classification datasets.
evaluations.result: Every reported dataset follows MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1; MHA/FC groups are above one and LayerNorm groups below one. ViT-Huge MHA is larger than ViT-Base MHA.
evaluations.baseline: Five native component groups, two ViT sizes, and the analytic bound order.

evaluations.setting: DINOv3-7B with ImageNet-22k/CIFAR-10 and GPT-2-124M with AG News/WikiText-103 proxy distributions.
evaluations.metric: Component plasticity distribution and depth trajectory.
evaluations.result: The descriptive MHA > FC1 > FC2 > normalization pattern is reproduced; no component-wise adaptation accuracy is reported.

evaluations.setting: ViT-Base, eleven full-data transfers, SGD with momentum 0.9, four dataset-specific learning rates, three seeds, classifier trained in every configuration.
evaluations.metric: Best validation-selected test top-1 accuracy, averaged over datasets.
evaluations.result: MHA 90.75, FC1 90.68, FC2 90.31, LN2 89.93, LN1 89.82; full fine-tuning 90.90 and linear probing 64.22.
evaluations.baseline: Full fine-tuning, linear probing, and four alternative component groups.

evaluations.setting: Same ViT-Base SGD matrix, inspecting all eleven Table 8 cells rather than only the aggregate.
evaluations.metric: Mean test top-1 accuracy over three seeds for each dataset/component pair.
evaluations.result: MHA is not the component winner on seven datasets; FC2 wins Sketch, LN2 wins Gaussian Noise and Flowers102, and LN1 wins Pets. Full fine-tuning has the best mean and wins four cells, while component tuning wins the other seven.

evaluations.setting: ViT-Base and ViT-Large on DomainNet Clipart.
evaluations.metric: Average test top-1 accuracy over the learning-rate grid.
evaluations.baseline: Five native component groups at 86M and 307M backbone scales.

evaluations.setting: ViT-Base on CIFAR-100, Motion Blur, Clipart, and Sketch using AdamW and a rate grid rescaled by 10^-2.
evaluations.metric: Average test top-1 accuracy over learning rates.
evaluations.result: Average MHA 82.2, FC1 81.4, FC2 81.7, LN2 79.4, LN1 79.2; variability is dataset-dependent and individual lower-ranked groups can win cells.
evaluations.baseline: The five component groups and the SGD ordering.

evaluations.setting: VTAB-style 1,000-example fine-tuning for 2,500 steps on Contrast, Motion Blur, Pets, Snow, and Sketch.
evaluations.metric: Average test top-1 accuracy over learning rates.
evaluations.baseline: The five component groups under the same low-data protocol.

evaluations.setting: ViT-Base theoretical bounds with n=197, H=12, and empirical mean token radius 19.4.
evaluations.metric: Numerically evaluated upper bound on component plasticity.
evaluations.result: The intended rank is obtained, but the attention bound remains around 10^6 and several orders above both other bounds and empirical plasticity scales.
evaluations.baseline: Empirical average expansion ratios and bounds for FC/LayerNorm.

evaluations.setting: Per-component training resource comparison on ViT-Base in FP32.
evaluations.metric: Trainable transformer parameters and gradient-plus-optimizer-state memory.
evaluations.result: MHA/FC1/FC2 each use 28M parameters and 220 MB; LN1/LN2 each use 18K and 0.14 MB.
evaluations.baseline: Equal-budget comparisons within the three large groups and within the two normalization groups.

limitations: [Author-stated] Tailored component-specific optimizers, learning rates, and schedulers remain future work.
[Author-stated] Decoder-only theory is outlined, but actual LLM component-adaptation experiments remain future work.
[Reviewer-inferred] P(f) measures response to input change, not capacity to change weights; the paper does not manipulate P(f) independently of component identity to establish causality.
[Reviewer-inferred] Calling P(f)>1 non-smooth conflates average expansion with differentiability and with worst-case/global Lipschitz properties.
[Reviewer-inferred] The theoretical rank compares upper bounds of radically different tightness, so it cannot order the underlying quantities without lower bounds or matched tightness results.
[Reviewer-inferred] The LayerNorm-versus-MHA/FC accuracy comparison is confounded by roughly 1,500-fold trainable-parameter and optimizer-memory differences.
[Reviewer-inferred] FC2 is evaluated on zero-padded embedded tokens rather than its native post-FC1/GeLU activation distribution.

[Reviewer-inferred] The central evidence is supervised image classification on ImageNet-pretrained ViTs; detection, segmentation, generative transfer, multimodal adaptation, and language adaptation are not evaluated.
[Reviewer-inferred] DINOv3 and GPT-2 support only the descriptive metric rank, not the claim that high-plasticity modules fine-tune better in those architectures.
[Reviewer-inferred] Only one ViT-Large component-fine-tuning dataset is reported and ViT-Huge is not fine-tuned component-wise.

[Reviewer-inferred] Three seeds and four rates provide useful coverage but no confidence intervals over the aggregate, correction for several component comparisons, or hierarchical treatment of heterogeneous datasets.
[Reviewer-inferred] The Wilcoxon test treats eleven datasets/corruptions as paired units even though five share CIFAR-10-C and therefore are not independent task draws.
[Reviewer-inferred] Robustness means stability across selected learning rates and seeds, not adversarial or distributional robustness despite the smoothness framing.
[Reviewer-inferred] The source/downstream pairing distribution is not shown to be invariant to embedding scale, sample balance, distance concentration, or the particular source corpus.
[Reviewer-inferred] The result-selected gradient trajectory in Figure 5 risks winner's-curse interpretation and is correlational.

[Reviewer-inferred] Full fine-tuning remains higher on the eleven-dataset mean, so the evidence supports prioritization under freezing constraints rather than a general performance advantage over full adaptation.

[Reviewer-inferred] A closely overlapping ICLR 2026 OpenReview submission reports attention and feed-forward normalization as most shift-sensitive and finds the sensitivity rank does not steadily predict component-tuning performance, leaving a direct unresolved empirical conflict.
failure_modes: A high average finite-difference ratio can reflect output scale or a few common directions without supplying useful task-gradient directions.
Selecting the highest-plasticity group may lose to FC1, FC2, LayerNorm, or full fine-tuning on an individual target dataset, as Table 8 already demonstrates.
Parameter-poor normalization groups may appear worse simply because they cannot express the target update, not because smoothness impedes learning.
Loose attention bounds can preserve the desired theoretical order even when actual component sensitivities do not follow it.
Zero-padding into FC2's 4d input can under- or over-estimate sensitivity relative to native nonlinear activations.
A rate grid tuned for broad comparability can miss the optimal schedule for small affine LayerNorm parameters or attention projections.
Pairing unrelated source/downstream examples can measure semantic/data-scale separation rather than local sensitivity to a controlled perturbation.
Distilled, instruction-tuned, post-normalized, gated, or alternative-attention transformers may reverse the reported order because the metric depends on learned weights and architecture.
High sensitivity may improve short-run optimization while worsening adversarial robustness, calibration, or stability; none of those trade-offs is measured.
Using aggregate task rank as a component-selection rule can obscure domain-specific winners and correlated benchmark families.
The classifier head is newly initialized in every component configuration, so its learning can dominate easy datasets and compress component differences.
DINOv3/GPT-2 proxy distribution choices can manufacture apparent cross-architecture consistency without matching the original pretraining distribution.
reusable_insights: Separate the measurable statement 'average expansion exceeds one' from claims about nondifferentiability, global smoothness, or robustness.
When using theoretical bounds to rank mechanisms, measure bound tightness and include lower bounds before treating the rank as explanatory.
Component-selection studies should parameter-match, optimizer-memory-match, and FLOP-match controls in addition to comparing native groups.
Evaluate a component on its native activation distribution; dimensional hacks such as zero-padding need a dedicated sensitivity audit.
Report the full per-task winner matrix because an aggregate rank is not a universal selection policy.
Distinguish descriptive cross-architecture replication from predictive validation by actually fine-tuning the measured components.
Use a factorial intervention: change sensitivity within a fixed module while holding trainable count, parameterization, initialization, and optimizer constant.
Treat source/downstream finite differences as distribution-dependent and report sensitivity to pair construction, normalization, and distance bins.
Compare component selection with gradient-based, angle-based, learned, and shift-type-based selectors under the same resource budget.
Pair optimization gains with adversarial, calibration, and stability measurements when recommending less-smooth components.
Use hierarchical statistics across dataset families rather than treating related corruptions as independent benchmarks.
Publish both accuracy-per-parameter and absolute accuracy; each answers a different adaptation question.
open_questions: Does plasticity still predict the best component after matching trainable parameters with repeated normalization parameters, low-rank attention/FC updates, or fixed-rank adapters?
Can sensitivity be manipulated within MHA or FC1 while preserving its function and budget, and does the intervention causally change fine-tuning speed or accuracy?
What rank is obtained when FC2 is evaluated on actual GeLU(FC1(x)) activations rather than zero-padded embedded tokens?
How stable is the rank to source corpus, target sample size, preprocessing, pair-distance strata, whitening, and feature rescaling?
Why does the near-direct ICLR 2026 sensitivity study rank feed-forward normalization highly while this paper ranks both norms lowest?
Do DINOv3, GPT-2, modern decoder LLMs, and multimodal transformers show the same relationship between measured plasticity and component-only adaptation outcomes?
Can tight or two-sided average-sensitivity bounds recover actual component magnitudes rather than only a visually convenient upper-bound order?
Does high component plasticity trade off against adversarial robustness, calibration, catastrophic forgetting, or training stability?
Can a target-aware selector outperform the fixed MHA/FC1 recommendation on datasets where FC2 or LayerNorm wins?
Does the conclusion persist under equalized hyperparameter-search budgets and component-specific optimal optimizers?
How does pretraining type, distillation, instruction tuning, normalization placement, gating, and token length change the rank?
Would multiple-comparison-aware hierarchical tests retain the claimed MHA advantage once correlated CIFAR-10-C variants are grouped?

competitive_landscape.title: Which Transformer Components Are the Most Sensitive to Distribution Shifts?
competitive_landscape.difference: This anonymous ICLR 2026 submission also decomposes ViTs, defines an averaged Lipschitz-style shift sensitivity, and fine-tunes components in isolation. It reports attention and feed-forward normalization as most sensitive, says higher sensitivity does not steadily predict performance across all blocks, and finds feed-forward normalization can match or surpass full fine-tuning at roughly 5,000x fewer parameters. That overlap and conflicting normalization result materially narrow the reviewed paper's novelty and demand a protocol-level reconciliation.

competitive_landscape.title: Partial Fine-Tuning: A Successor to Full Fine-Tuning for Vision Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: It evaluates eight partial ViT strategies, already finds FFN-only or attention-only tuning can outperform full fine-tuning, and selects layers with a fine-tuned-angle metric. The reviewed paper adds an input-sensitivity explanation and module-level rank, but does not compare its selector head-to-head with the angle criterion under a matched budget.

competitive_landscape.title: Three things everyone should know about Vision Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: It establishes that attention-only fine-tuning can adapt ViTs to new resolution and classification tasks while saving memory and compute. The reviewed paper broadens the native component comparison and proposes plasticity as an explanation, so attention-only effectiveness itself is not novel.

competitive_landscape.title: Surgical Fine-Tuning Improves Adaptation to Distribution Shifts
competitive_landscape.difference: Surgical fine-tuning shows that the best contiguous layer subset depends on whether shift is at the input, feature, or output level and provides gradient-based selectors. The reviewed paper proposes a global component-type priority from sensitivity, but its own per-dataset exceptions are consistent with Surgical Fine-Tuning's target-dependent view.

competitive_landscape.title: Tuning LayerNorm in Attention: Towards Efficient Multi-Modal LLM Finetuning
competitive_landscape.difference: It reports that tuning only LayerNorm can outperform LoRA and full tuning for multimodal LLM adaptation with as little as 0.004% trainable parameters. The task and architecture differ, but it is a direct counterexample to treating low measured norm plasticity as generally undesirable for adaptation.

competitive_landscape.title: Exploiting Layer Normalization Fine-tuning in Visual Transformer Foundation Models for Classification
competitive_landscape.difference: This vision-specific study models LayerNorm parameter shifts under data scarcity and domain shift and improves LayerNorm tuning by FSR-conditioned rescaling. It suggests norm adaptation quality depends on target representativeness, a target-dependent variable absent from the reviewed fixed rank.

competitive_landscape.title: Sensitivity-Aware Visual Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: SPT also uses parameter sensitivity to decide where and how to adapt a ViT, then applies unstructured or structured updates. Its sensitivity is parameter/task-loss based rather than input-output expansion, making it an essential predictive-selector baseline missing from the reviewed experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling & Shifting Your Features: A New Baseline for Efficient Model Tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: SSF learns small feature-wise scales and shifts, can be merged at inference, and reports gains over full fine-tuning across 26 classification datasets plus robustness/OOD tests. It makes the reviewed native LayerNorm result an incomplete proxy for what parameter-matched affine feature adaptation can achieve.

competitive_landscape.title: Visual Prompt Tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: VPT adapts frozen ViTs through a small number of learned input tokens and reports competitive transfer with under 1% task-specific parameters. It changes no native component, so it is an orthogonal accuracy-per-parameter baseline that the component-rank study does not evaluate directly.

competitive_landscape.title: ExPLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Extended Pre-Training to Adapt Vision Transformers under Domain Shifts
competitive_landscape.difference: ExPLoRA unfreezes one or two ViT blocks while applying LoRA elsewhere during self-supervised domain continuation, then fine-tunes with LoRA. It targets severe domain shift and combines block choice with low-rank updates rather than claiming one native component type is universally preferable.

competitive_landscape.title: Canonical Rank Adaptation: An Efficient Fine-Tuning Strategy for Vision Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: CaRA tensorizes MHA projection and feed-forward weights and applies CP-decomposition low-rank adaptation, directly exploiting the component structures highlighted by the reviewed paper while controlling trainable rank. It is a stronger resource-matched adaptation comparator than full native 28M-component updates.

competitive_landscape.title: How Smooth Is Attention?
competitive_landscape.difference: It supplies tight local Lipschitz scaling for bounded unmasked and masked self-attention, including a mean-field regime. The reviewed paper builds on those tools but evaluates much looser weight-dependent bounds and turns them into an adaptation rank that Castin et al. do not claim.

competitive_landscape.title: The Lipschitz Constant of Self-Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: It proves standard dot-product self-attention is not globally Lipschitz on an unbounded domain and proposes Lipschitz L2 attention. This result forces the reviewed paper's bounded-input assumptions and shows why its finite sample average cannot be read as a global smoothness certificate.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Transformers with Enforced Lipschitz Constants
competitive_landscape.difference: This work directly intervenes on Transformer Lipschitz bounds and finds a severe smoothness-performance trade-off: matching a 145M NanoGPT baseline requires an enormous reported bound. It supports the possibility that excessive smoothness hurts capacity, but does not validate the reviewed paper's component-level proxy or causal rank.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Layer Selection for Efficient Vision Transformer Fine-Tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: ALaST reallocates compute by estimating layer importance at each minibatch, freezing low-budget layers and reducing their tokens, with reported training, FLOP, and memory reductions. It is target- and time-adaptive, whereas the reviewed paper recommends a fixed across-depth component group from a precomputed sensitivity rank.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a novel perspective in which high average input-output plasticity, hence lower smoothness, explains which Transformer components should be prioritized for fine-tuning, supported by component bounds and more than one thousand ViT runs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper contributes a concrete distribution-averaged finite-difference measurement over native ViT components, verifies a stable descriptive order across eleven datasets and multiple backbones, and supplies a large component-only optimization matrix with SGD, Adam, low-data, and gradient-dynamics checks.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is moderate and concentrated in the particular P(f) metric plus its empirical/theoretical packaging, not in attention/FFN-only tuning or sensitivity-guided selection. Attention-only tuning, partial fine-tuning, surgical selection, LayerNorm tuning, and parameter-sensitivity selectors predate it. Most importantly, OpenReview rwmUsy4ClE poses a nearly identical averaged-Lipschitz component-sensitivity question and reaches a conflicting conclusion about normalization; until the relationship and protocol differences are clarified, broad priority and first-perspective claims should be treated cautiously. The bounds motivate but do not prove the empirical rank, and capacity confounding prevents a causal smoothness conclusion.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text pass over all 60 extracted pages, including related work, proofs, implementation, complete per-dataset tables, robustness/gradient figures, Adam results, and reproducibility/carbon appendix. Source hash corresponds to the locally indexed export.arxiv.org PDF; arXiv current record was checked on 2026-08-23 as arXiv:2602.06883v3 (revised 2026-06-03). Competitor search covered native component tuning, sensitivity/layer selection, LayerNorm counterexamples, modern ViT PEFT, and attention/Lipschitz theory using only arXiv, OpenReview, CVF, NeurIPS, and PMLR primary records. Numerical table values were transcribed from Table 8/TeX where PDF text-column ordering was lossy. Confidence is high for what is reported and for the explicit parameter/bound/FC2-input contradictions; confidence in the causal interpretation is materially lower because no matched intervention isolates plasticity.
